title: Antivirus False Positive Tracker – False Positive Heroes
description: Public record of antivirus false positives on an independent developer’s software: VirusTotal observations, detection-days by engine, and current false positives.
headline:
There was no virus.
Still a hit.
intro:
A hall of fame for antivirus engines that flagged perfectly harmless software.
With each false positive, an independent developer loses users’ trust and has to start explaining.
award:
Can’t find a threat?
Why not make one up?
awardText:
Where detection counts are read as performance,
even a false positive goes on the scorecard.
We record those false positives and how they are handled afterwards.

methodTitle: Even one false positive does harm when it lingers.
methodDesc: Before rankings: consistent criteria and verifiable evidence.
m1: {files} files from software the developer has published are monitored through VirusTotal. This is a record of false positives and detection burden on this sample, from the developer’s perspective; it does not represent any engine’s overall performance. Policy-based detections (PUA, Riskware, etc.) that flag a program as potentially unwanted rather than malicious are not counted.
m2: Score = total detection duration across files divided by 24 hours. One file flagged for a day earns one point. Ongoing cases count up to the cutoff. Monthly scores count only duration falling within that month.
m3title: No response does not mean cleared
m3: Duration runs from the first observed detection to the first observation confirming a clean result. Each false positive is reported to the vendor as soon as it is found, so the duration includes the time it stayed after being reported. Actual onset and clearance times may differ. An engine not responding is not treated as clearance; cases with unconfirmed clearance keep accumulating in the provisional score. An unconfirmed clearance is confirmed at the first later scan in which at least as many engines respond and the detection is absent. Files excluded from monitoring (replaced by a new version or no longer distributed) stop counting at their last scan.
disclaimer: The wording on this page expresses an opinion about an evaluation structure centered on detection counts. It does not assert the intent of any specific vendor. All figures are based on observation records.
missionTitle:
The antivirus: one false positive.
The developer: dozens of lines of explanation.
missionText:
Users stop downloading. Software gets deleted. The developer is suspected of writing malware. The cost of a false positive falls more on whoever made the software than on the antivirus that got it wrong.

This page does not evaluate the overall detection performance of any antivirus. It publicly documents misjudgments of legitimate software and the responses that follow, to reduce the harm to independent developers.
harmTitle: When false positives spread, PCs and work stop.
harmText: When an antivirus wrongly flags Windows system files or legitimate programs and quarantines, deletes or blocks them, the damage is real: PCs that will not boot or keep rebooting, banking and public services knocked offline, even leaked documents. Every case below happened and made the news. A false positive is not just the developer’s problem; it is a risk to every user’s PC and work.
harmList:
• 2006McAfeeFlagged Excel and other Office components, Java, Flash and more, and deleted them → apps had to be reinstalledThe Register ↗
  • 2007Symantec (Norton)Flagged Windows XP system files (netapi32.dll, lsasrv.dll) on Chinese PCs → PCs failed to bootComputerworld ↗
  • 2008AvastFlagged a Korean online-banking security program (nProtect) → deleting it left some PCs unbootable, requiring Windows reinstallsMoney Today (Korean) ↗
  • 2008AhnLab V3Deleted lsass.exe from Windows XP → PCs failed to bootKyunghyang Shinmun (Korean) ↗
  • 2008AVGFlagged user32.dll in Windows XP → endless rebootsArs Technica ↗
  • 2009McAfeeFlagged a keyboard-security program used for online banking → customers of a Korean bank (SC First Bank) could not bank onlineElectronic Times (Korean) ↗
  • 2009AvastFlagged programs built with Delphi/C++Builder en masse (archivers, Skype, brokerage trading apps) and deleted them → work disruptedKuki News (Korean) ↗
  • 2010AhnLab V3Flagged government administration programs (resident registration system) as spyware and blocked them → Korea’s nationwide civil-service network went downiNews24 (Korean) ↗
  • 2010BitDefenderFlagged system files on 64-bit Windows → PCs failed to bootArs Technica ↗
  • 2010McAfeeFlagged svchost.exe → reboot loops on enterprise PCs worldwideThe Register ↗
  • 2011AhnLab V3Flagged legitimate files; cleaning also deleted system files → boot failuresHankyoreh (Korean) ↗
  • 2011Microsoft Security EssentialsFlagged Google Chrome as malware (Zbot) and removed it → Chrome deleted from many PCs; Google shipped an emergency fixWIRED ↗
  • 2012SophosFlagged its own and other vendors’ updaters → many corporate PCs could no longer update; admins had to fix each PC by handZDNET ↗
  • 2013MalwarebytesFlagged Windows system files → unstable systems, some unable to bootThe Register ↗
  • 2015PandaQuarantined its own files and Windows system32 files → PCs unusableThe Register ↗
  • 2017WebrootQuarantined Windows system files and hundreds of business apps → servers and PCs stopped workingArs Technica ↗
  • 2022ESTsecurity ALYacFlagged built-in Windows processes as ransomware → frozen PCs that would not boot; small businesses could not take ordersNewsis (Korean) ↗
  • 2025Microsoft DefenderFlagged Adobe Acrobat Cloud document links as malicious → companies checking them uploaded 1,700+ sensitive documents to a public sandboxCybernews ↗
  • 2026Microsoft DefenderFlagged DigiCert root certificates as a trojan and removed them from Windows → some users reinstalled Windows thinking they were infectedBleepingComputer ↗
